replying_to: Replying to Towards an AI Musician: Synthesizing Sheet Music Problems for Musical Reasoning
display_title: Official Review of Submission11456 by Reviewer D6f4

summary.value: This paper proposes a benchmark for reasoning on synthetic music sheets, leveraging synthetic data created through reinforcement learning. This is combined with experiments across LLMs and MLLMs, also showing how models also have abilities beyond reasoning in music composition.

strengths.value:
* The problem of reasoning on music sheets is relatively unexplored, and the contribution of leveraging music theory rules to synthesize sheet music is sufficiently novel.
* Experimental results across various LLMs and MLLMs are well constructed and cover textual QA as well as visual QA plus benchmarks on real-world data.

weaknesses.value:
* Some assumptions made in this work are not clarified in the paper, and some design choices are not presented with sufficient clarity - see the below section for details.
* The resulting synthetic data are still fairly simple from a musical point of view and might not scale to complex compositions, or to noisy and degraded images of scores or even handwritten notation.
* The manuscript includes very few critical remarks arguing on the strengths and weaknesses of the proposed benchmark and offers no clear avenues for future work, therefore limiting the scholarly quality of the paper.

questions.value:
* Section 1 and 2.1 make several claims that "sheet music is the universal language" which are not correct from a musical or musicological point of view. This work uses a particular form of music notation (namely Western staff notation) but not all music cultures use this type of notation, and not all music cultures use music notation in the first place. Even some styles within Western music use alternative forms of notation, e.g. guitar tabs. Therefore the scope of this work needs to be revised accordingly and certain assumptions made regarding the data (and theory) domain would need to be clarified.
* Some aspects of this work involve converting ABC notation to images. This conversion process can have significant effects on performance for visual QA tasks, however there is no information provided on which notation-to-image engraving method was used, and there appears to not have been any work on using different engraving methods as to improve the diversity of the image data.
* From Figure 4 the composition of the test set appears to cover questions related to Chords, Scale, Intervals, and Rhythm. One question might be: are these 4 categories sufficient to claim understanding and reasoning for sheet music? Which musical aspects might be missing from these questions which could form a new benchmark?
* Table 2: what is the "Thinking" column?
* In section 4.1, there are comparisons with real-world benchmarks. For MMMU Music and the Visual QA task, it appears that the table only shows results using the proposed method. How is performance when compared with reported results and other methods using the MMMU benchmark and specifically its Visual QA task?
* Section 6 only provides a limited summary of the paper. Instead this could have provided some critical remarks on this work, emphasizing on the strengths but also the areas of possible improvement for this work, combined with directions of future work. Currently there is limited critical material on this paper which limits its scholarly contribution.

Thank you for your insightful feedback. We will address each of these points individually.
### Weakness

1. Some assumptions made in this work are not clarified in the paper, and some design choices are not presented with sufficient clarity - see the below section for details.
    
    Thank you for the insightful feedback. We will revise our paper accordingly, as the following responses.
    
2. The resulting synthetic data are still fairly simple from a musical point of view and might not scale to complex compositions, or to noisy and degraded images of scores or even handwritten notation.
    
    
    Thank you for this important comment. Our current framework focuses on the foundational, local rules of music theory. We agree that our initial claim of “full sheet music reasoning” was an overstatement, and we will revise it throughout the manuscript to the more precise term “foundational musical reasoning”. 
    
    This work represents the crucial first step in our research roadmap. We began with these foundational domains because the rules are deterministic, allowing us to develop and validate our data synthesis pipeline with a high degree of confidence.
    
    For higher-level concepts like harmonic progression or musical form, we can indeed leverage powerful tools like music21 to develop programmatic synthesis algorithms. However, the complexity and stylistic nuance of these rules mean that the correctness of the synthesis algorithms themselves must be rigorously validated. 
    
    Therefore, this next stage requires a thorough black-box testing phase involving a panel of music experts to certify that our synthesis algorithms are musically sound across a wide range of examples. Before committing to this expert-led validation effort, it was imperative for us to first demonstrate that the underlying RLVR training paradigm is effective for musical tasks.
    
    Regarding the conversion of scores or handwritten notation, we believe this is outside the current scope of our work. Users can independently generate their own style-specific image representations from ABC notation, which can then be used to create diverse datasets. While the exploration of image synthesis and augmentation methods for these images is an interesting and valuable direction, it represents a separate line of research that our work aims to inspire in the future.
    
    Finally, we present the details of our roadmap, next steps, and technical plan for your review of the feasibility addressed in our response to Weakness 3. We look forward to receiving your insightful feedback.

3. The manuscript includes very few critical remarks arguing on the strengths and weaknesses of the proposed benchmark and offers no clear avenues for future work, therefore limiting the scholarly quality of the paper.

    Thank you for this constructive suggestion. We agree that providing a transparent critique of our current limitations and outlining a clear path forward significantly enhances the scholarly quality of the work.
    To address this, we will add a new section, "Section 6: Limitations and Future Work," to the revised manuscript. In this section, we critically analyze the current focus on local, rule-based synthetics and share our research roadmap to guide the community:

    ---
    
    **Foundational Musical Reasoning. (QA) (This work)**
    
    This initial work was all about ensuring the model masters the fundamental "grammar" of music theory. Before understanding musical ideas, it must correctly identify non-negotiable errors like incorrect rhythm. At the same time, this work aims to explore the feasibility and potential of this direction, offering a new avenue for further research.
    
    **Higher-Level Structural and Harmonic Reasoning.  (QA) (Next Step)**
    
    Our next step, which is our current focus, is to teach the model to reason about musical structure. To do this, we will leverage the **Music21** toolkit. Its analytical capabilities allow us to parse sheet music and generate clear, objective "ground truth" data. This enables us to automatically create a series of verifiable questions that rigorously test the model's ability to reason about high-level structures, such as harmonic progressions. At this stage, we also require additional expert professionals to validate the accuracy of the generation algorithm through black-box testing.
    
    Besides, a key goal of the second stage is to engineer a systematic Python package. This framework will be designed to synthesize musical reasoning problems from low to high levels. We plan to build it with good software engineering principles, create an extensible question types, and invite the research community to contribute. We believe building a true AI musician requires a passionate, collaborative effort.
    
    **Sheet Music Creation. (Generation & QA) (Final Step)**
    
    Once the model can reliably analyze and understand musical structure, the final and most exciting stage is to have it start creating its own. This is where we shift from analysis to generation.  In this stage, we will move beyond objective judgment, although we have not yet fully decided on the approach to achieve this.
    
    **Others**
    
    While this roadmap outlines our specific path forward, we believe this work can inspire a range of valuable research directions for the community, including:
    
    1. Extending to develop automated methods for converting standard staff notation into other symbolic formats (e.g., tablature, lead sheets, or ABC notation). 
    2. Designing image synthesis methods that generate scores with human-like stylistic handwriting variations  from abc notation becomes very important and meaningful work. It can help MLLMs to generalize to real-world, "in-the-wild" scenarios, such as analyzing scores from smartphone photos or scanned historical documents. 
    3. Beyond the visual domain, sheet music is a symbolic representation that can be programmatically rendered into other modalities, such as MIDI (performance data) and audio (sound). This allows for the creation of large-scale, perfectly aligned, multi-modal datasets.
    
    Since the underlying musical logic remains consistent across different notations and modalities, our paradigm could be used to generate parallel corpora of multi-format and multi-modal scores with identical ground-truth data. This verifiable consistency is particularly valuable for RLVR, enabling scalable reinforcement learning of musical understanding across diverse modalities and notations. All these potential research directions can be integrated into our system, making it a foundational tool for the research community.
    
    ---
    
    We believe our work can inspire a wide range of future research, and we will include a section that provides detailed guidance for others to follow our approach.

While we believe the broader term "sheet music" can encompass various systems, including the excellent example of guitar tablature you provided, our current framework is specifically designed for the rule-based structure of staff notation. The use of the phrase "universal language" was indeed an oversimplification, and we appreciate you bringing this inaccuracy to our attention. We will revise this accordingly.
    
2. Some aspects of this work involve converting ABC notation to images. This conversion process can have significant effects on performance for visual QA tasks, however there is no information provided on which notation-to-image engraving method was used, and there appears to not have been any work on using different engraving methods as to improve the diversity of the image data.
    
    
    To address your first point, we will ensure this is highlighted more clearly in the manuscript. As mentioned on page 3 (line 160), our process is a two-step pipeline:
    
    - First, we use the abcm2ps library to convert the ABC notation into a high-quality vector image.
    - Then, we use ImageMagick to render this into a standard image format for the visual QA tasks.
    
     We will make this information more prominent in our experimental setup section to ensure full reproducibility.
    
    On the other hand, you are absolutely correct that for real-world applications, models must generalize to a wide variety of visual renderings. This can be achieved by altering fonts, typefaces, spacing, and so on, as well as incorporating traditional computer vision data augmentation methods to enhance data diversity. However, this was not the focus of our current paper.  We plan to incorporate these aspects into the next tool in our work, as part of our shared research plan.
    
3. From Figure 4 the composition of the test set appears to cover questions related to Chords, Scale, Intervals, and Rhythm. One question might be: are these 4 categories sufficient to claim understanding and reasoning for sheet music? Which musical aspects might be missing from these questions which could form a new benchmark?
    
    
    Thank you for your insightful question regarding the scope of question types. Our four categories of Chords, Scale, Intervals, and Rhythm represent the foundational level of musical literacy. While essential, they are not sufficient on their own to constitute comprehensive musical reasoning, which we aim to address in the next phase. In response to weaknesses 2&3, we have outlined our research plan and technical details. We will add a section discussing limitations and future work. We also look forward to collaborating with the research community to advance the development of AI musician. 
    
4. Table 2: what is the "Thinking" column?
    
    
    The "Thinking" column indicates whether the reasoning mode is activated in a reasoning model. For some models, the reasoning mode can be turned off, and we use the term "thinking" to specify when it is enabled. We acknowledge that this point was not sufficiently clear in the original manuscript and will revise it to better convey this limitation.

summary.value: This paper introduces a new benchmark that generates sheet-music reasoning problems in text and image form based on core music-theory rules (N=1600 + 8000 each). The main application of this benchmark is to train LLM/VLM to reason about sheet music. The paper shows that using this synthetic data for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards improves LLMs performance on the given benchmark, as well as on two existing benchmarks, MusicTheoryBench and MMMU.

strengths.value:
Programmatic pipeline for synthetic data generation allows a principled generation of a large number of problems, allowing to generate a much larger benchmark compared to existing ones.

The benchmark is novel, and includes diverse question types.

Beyond music, the pattern “encode domain rules -> synthesize verifiable tasks -> RLVR” is general and timely for reasoning-centric training

 The expert-templated, rules-driven generator produces auto-graded, controllable items (bar placement, interval/chord/scale families), and deterministically renders images. This is ideal for RLVR where reward correctness matters.

A wide a range of state-of-the-art LLMs and MLLMs are included in the evaluation

weaknesses.value:
Presentation clarity. 

Dataset only focuses on 4 music theory domains (scale, rhythm, interval, chord). The questions are focused on music theory rule application, wheres for a reasoning benchmark it would be good to consider tasks such as inferring key modulations or harmonic function given a progression, which involve integrating symbolic, structural, and contextual information. 

Even a small study comparing how the best-performing fine-tuned models perform compared to humans would be useful.

questions.value:
Are there existing non-LLM based models that can solve these reasoning problems?

How was the specific given subset of reasoning questions chosen to be included in the benchmark?

comment.value:
2. Even a small study comparing how the best-performing fine-tuned models perform compared to humans would be useful.

        
    Thank you for the valuable suggestion. We carefully considered including a human control study. However, it is important to note that the tasks in our dataset (e.g., interval identification, rhythm counting) correspond to axiomatic music theory rules where the "ground truth" is mathematically defined.

    For a trained musician, these tasks are foundational, and human performance effectively hits a "ceiling" of near 100% accuracy. Consequently, a quantitative comparison would not yield significant statistical insight. The core challenge addressed in this paper is not whether the model can purely match human accuracy, but whether it can internalize the reasoning process of a musician.
    
    To illustrate this, we present a case from our Qwen2.5-7B-Base+GRPO model. As shown below, the model does not simply guess the answer; it simulates the exact cognitive workflow a human musician uses to analyze a score:

    **example**: 

    ```
    L:1/8
    Q:1/4=120
    M:3/4
    K:F
    f4 F2 g2 gg gg g4 G2 a2 ba gf
    ```

    **model response**:

    ```
    To determine the correct placement of bar lines in the given sequence of notes, we need to consider the time signature, which is 3/4 in this case. This means each measure must contain exactly three quarter notes (or the equivalent).

    Let's analyze the sequence of notes:

    L:1/8
    Q:1/4=120
    M:3/4
    K:F
    f4 F2 g2 gg gg g4 G2 a2 ba gf

    Breaking it down into smaller segments:

    1. f4 F2
    2. g2 gg gg
    3. g4 G2
    4. a2 ba gf

    Each segment should contain exactly three quarter notes. Let's count the quarter notes in each segment:

    1. f4 F2: 4 (f) + 2 (F) = 6 eighth notes
    2. g2 gg gg: 2 (g) + 2 (gg) + 2 (gg) = 6 eighth notes
    3. g4 G2: 4 (g) + 2 (G) = 6 eighth notes
    4. a2 ba gf: 2 (a) + 2 (ba) + 2 (gf) = 6 eighth notes

    Since the time signature is 3/4, each measure must contain exactly three quarter notes. Therefore, the correct placement of bar lines would be after the first and third segments, as they each contain exactly three quarter notes.

    The correct option is:

    A. L:1/8
    Q:1/4=120
    M:3/4
    K:F
    | f4 F2 | g2 gg gg | g4 G2 | a2 ba gf |

    So, the answer is \boxed{A}.
    ```

    These reasoning abilities are foundational skills, essential for LLMs to compose sheet music in a manner akin to human musicians.


### Question

1. Are there existing non-LLM based models that can solve these reasoning problems?
    
    Thank you for this question. Yes, traditional symbolic algorithms and encoder-only models (like BERT) can indeed solve these specific multiple-choice questions with high accuracy.

    However, the objective of this work is not merely to calculate the correct answers, but to enable LLMs to "think" like musicians. While discriminative models are efficient, they cannot explain why an answer is correct in natural language, nor can they apply that knowledge to generate new music.
    
    By training an LLM to internalize these rules through explicit reasoning rather than simple classification, we aim to bridge the gap between rigid rule-based systems and the creative, generative capabilities required for future AI musicians.


2. How was the specific given subset of reasoning questions chosen to be included in the benchmark?
    
    Thank you for your question. We randomly sampled 400 questions from each category, resulting in a test set of 1,600 questions. The remaining questions were used to construct the training set. Both datasets can be converted into a visual QA format.

display_title: Official Review of Submission11456 by Reviewer CAkk

summary.value: This paper proposes a synthetic data generation framework that converts core music theory rules (rhythm, interval, chord, scale) into programmable functions for producing verifiable sheet-music reasoning problems. The authors introduce SSMR-Bench, consisting of 3,200 evaluation QA pairs (text + image) and a larger 16K training set for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). They show that training on synthetic musical reasoning data improves performance on SSMR-Bench, and also transfers to existing human-crafted benchmarks such as MusicTheoryBench and MMMU-Music. The paper further claims that the learned reasoning ability benefits symbolic music composition.

strengths.value:
Novel data synthesis idea.
Treating music theory as a rule-based generator of reasoning problems is conceptually parallel to math problem synthesis, and enables scalable, verifiable QA generation.

Benchmark + training pipeline.
The paper contributes both an evaluation benchmark and a synthetic training dataset, filling a gap for sheet-music reasoning tasks.

Demonstrated improvements on multiple models.
RLVR-trained Qwen models show clear gains on SSMR-Bench and moderate gains on MusicTheoryBench and MMMU-Music.

Cross-domain effect is interesting.
The observation that music reasoning training may improve math reasoning hints at shared symbolic reasoning structure.

weaknesses.value:
Music theory coverage is limited.
The synthesis only covers local rules (rhythm, interval, chord, scale) and does not address global musical structure, harmonic progression, voice-leading, or form—so the claim of “full sheet music reasoning” is overstated.

Performance still far from SOTA baselines.
Although training improves scores, the models still lag well behind state-of-the-art on MusicTheoryBench, suggesting limited real-world transfer.

MMMU results close to random guessing.
On MMMU-Music, accuracy remains near the 25% random baseline, indicating the model may mainly learn QA format rather than visual score reasoning.

Composition evaluation is narrow.
The “improved music composition” result only tests 4-bar rhythmic alignment with prompt tempo, ignoring key musical elements such as harmonic coherence, chord progression, or longer-term structure.

Minor but NOTABLE typo.
“GRPO” is repeatedly misspelled as GPRO in Lines 208–216.

questions.value:
Music theory scope
Do you plan to extend synthesis to higher-level rules (e.g., cadences, phrase structure, functional harmony, chord progression)? If not, how should readers interpret the term sheet music reasoning?

Math transfer claim
In Sec. 4.2, you suggest music reasoning helps math reasoning. Can you test whether music+math mixed training outperforms “math-only extra epochs”?

Benchmark gap
Why do models still underperform SOTA on MusicTheoryBench despite large synthetic training? Is the gap due to missing global theory features?

MMMU near-random accuracy
Can you provide an ablation to show whether the model is learning symbolic reasoning or just answer-pattern priors?

Composition evaluation
Would you consider adding harmonic correctness or chord adherence metrics, instead of only rhythm-based alignment?

Annotation correctness
Are the synthetic questions automatically validated? If so, what is the estimated error rate of the generation pipeline?

    Thank you for this sharp observation regarding the MMMU results. You are correct that the performance, even after training, is modest in absolute terms. However, we argue that this is not due to the model merely learning the QA format, but is instead a realistic measure of the profound difficulty of this specific benchmark, which validates the need for our work.
    
    To properly contextualize these results, it is crucial to consider the performance of state-of-the-art MLLMs. As recent benchmarks show, **Gemini-2.5-Pro**, a model might be hundreds or even thousands of times larger than our 7B model, achieves only **36.67%** accuracy on MMMU-Music. This highlights that this is an exceptionally challenging task that even the most powerful generalist models struggle with.
    
    This industry-wide difficulty is, we argue, a direct symptom of the very problem our paper addresses: **the scarcity of large-scale, verifiable training data for sheet music reasoning.** Regarding the concern that the model is only learning the format, our **6.67% absolute improvement** (from 20.00% to 26.67%) demonstrates a genuine, albeit nascent, enhancement in reasoning.  
    
    To further illustrate the symbolic reasoning, consider the following case from Qwen2.5-VL-7B-IT+GRPO. While we are unable to include the image, we will present the question and the response:
    
    > Q: <image 1> The second measure of the above example uses which rhythmic device?
    > 
    > 
    >        A. 'Anacrusis' B. 'Hemiola'  C. 'Suspension'  D. 'Augmentation'
    > 
    
    > A: To determine the correct answer, let's analyze the rhythm in the second measure of the given musical example:
    > 
    > 
    > The first two notes in the second measure are on the third beat of the measure, and the next two notes are on the fourth beat of the measure. This creates a pattern where the first two beats of the measure are divided into three notes instead of the usual two.
    > 
    > This is characteristic of a hemiola, where a regular meter is temporarily altered by having a group of three notes where there would normally be only two.
    > 
    > Therefore, the correct answer is:
    > \boxed{B}
    > 
    
    Ultimately, these findings—both the improvement and the remaining challenge—validate our methodology and illuminate a clear direction for future research.
    
4. Composition evaluation is narrow. The “improved music composition” result only tests 4-bar rhythmic alignment with prompt tempo, ignoring key musical elements such as harmonic coherence, chord progression, or longer-term structure.
    
    
    Thank you for this excellent suggestion. To address your point, we have added a new evaluation for harmonic correctness using the **Chord Tone to non-Chord Tone Ratio (CTnCTR)[1,2]**. This metric calculates the percentage of a melody that consists of either stable chord tones or smoothly resolving non-chord tones.

     $$\text{CTnCTR} = \frac{n_c + n_p}{\text{Total Notes}}$$
    
    - $n_c$ (Chord Tones): Notes belonging to the current triad (Root, 3rd, 5th).
    - $n_p$ (Proper Non-Chord Tones): Non-chord notes that are exactly 2 semitones (a whole step) away from the immediate next note.
    
    We present the results, along with our findings on rhythm consistency, below.
    
    |  | CTnCTR | RC |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | Qwen3-8B-Base | 88.03% | 59.00% |
    | Qwen3-8B-Base+GRPO Music | **91.21%** | **76.00%** |
    | Qwen3-8B-Thinking | 88.11% | 61.50% |
    
    The results show that our model trained with synthetic music data (+GRPO Music) achieves the highest score, indicating that our training approach also enhances the model's ability to generate harmonically coherent melodies.
    
    [1]Wu S, Yang Y, Wang Z, et al. Generating chord progression from melody with flexible harmonic rhythm and controllable harmonic density[J]. EURASIP Journal on Audio, Speech, and Music Processing, 2024, 2024(1): 4.
    
    [2]Wu S, Wang Y, Li X, et al. Melodyt5: A unified score-to-score transformer for symbolic music processing[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.02277, 2024.
    
5. Minor but NOTABLE typo. “GRPO” is repeatedly misspelled as GPRO in Lines 208–216
    
    Thank you for pointing this out. We have corrected the typo in the revised manuscript.

    ---
    **Foundational Musical Reasoning. (QA) (This work)**
    
    This initial work was all about ensuring the model masters the fundamental "grammar" of music theory. Before understanding musical ideas, it must correctly identify non-negotiable errors like incorrect rhythm. We see this as the essential groundwork, creating a solid, verifiably correct foundation upon which all future capabilities will be built.
    
    **Higher-Level Structural and Harmonic Reasoning.  (QA) (Next Step)**
    
    Our next step, which is our current focus, is to teach the model to reason about musical structure. To do this, we will leverage the **Music21** toolkit. Its analytical capabilities allow us to parse sheet music and generate clear, objective "ground truth" data. This enables us to automatically create a series of verifiable questions that rigorously test the model's ability to reason about high-level structures, such as harmonic progressions. At this stage, we also require additional expert professionals to validate the accuracy of the generation algorithm through black-box testing.

    Besides, a key goal of the second stage is to engineer a systematic Python package. This framework will be designed to synthesize musical reasoning problems from low to high levels. We plan to build it with good software engineering principles, create an extensible question types, and invite the research community to contribute. We believe building a true AI musician requires a passionate, collaborative effort.
    
    **Sheet Music Creation. (Generation & QA) (Final Step)**
    
    Once the model can reliably analyze and understand musical structure, the final and most exciting stage is to have it start creating its own. This is where we shift from analysis to generation.  In this stage, we will move beyond objective judgment, although we have not yet fully decided on the approach to achieve this.
    
    **Others**
    
    While this roadmap outlines our specific path forward, we believe this work can inspire a range of valuable research directions for the community, including:
    
    1. Extending to develop automated methods for converting standard staff notation into other symbolic formats (e.g., tablature, lead sheets, or ABC notation). 
    2. Designing image synthesis methods that generate scores with human-like stylistic handwriting variations from abc notation becomes very important and meaningful work. It can help MLLMs to generalize to real-world, "in-the-wild" scenarios, such as analyzing scores from smartphone photos or scanned historical documents. 
    3. Beyond the visual domain, sheet music is a symbolic representation that can be programmatically rendered into other modalities, such as MIDI (performance data) and audio (sound). This allows for the creation of large-scale, perfectly aligned, multi-modal datasets.
    
    Since the underlying musical logic remains consistent across different notations and modalities, our paradigm could be used to generate parallel corpora of multi-format and multi-modal scores with identical ground-truth data. This verifiable consistency is particularly valuable for RLVR, enabling scalable reinforcement learning of musical understanding across diverse modalities and notations. All these potential research directions can be integrated into our system, making it a foundational tool for the research community.

---

    **1. On the Framework's Core Function (Generating Questions, not Music)**
    
    You are correct in your assessment that our framework **generates verifiable questions from existing, real-world sheet music**, rather than synthesizing the music itself. This is a deliberate design choice central to our primary goal: creating a resource for the **Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)** paradigm. The framework is built upon programmatic functions that encode rules from four fundamental domains: **Rhythm, Chord, Interval, and Scale**, which encompass nine distinct question templates. For instance, our "NoteCompletionByInterval" template programmatically applies the rules of interval calculation, while "ChordKeyRootIdentification" tests the principles of triadic harmony.

This section will fully describe the algorithm and the specific music theory rules encoded in each of the nine question templates. We will then explicitly reference this appendix in Section 2.2 to ensure the core mechanics of our framework are clear and transparent.

Our intention was to draw an analogy to mathematics, where a finite set of simple operations (e.g., addition) can generate a virtually infinite number of unique problems from the universe of numbers. Similarly, our framework applies a core set of music theory rules to a massive corpus of sheet music (e.g., the MelodyHub dataset).

2. Although the paper claims to address musical reasoning, the current questions do not appear to require genuine reasoning. According to Appendix A, all questions are recognition/identification of local features (e.g., scale, chord, interval). That fits “sheet-music understanding,” but it is not reasoning in the stronger sense as in Yue et al. 2024.
    
    Thank you for this insightful point. It seems the paper link was inadvertently omitted. We assume you are referring to the MMMU benchmark paper.
    
    You have articulated a key philosophical distinction about the nature of reasoning versus understanding. The most intuitive way to distinguish these tasks from simple recognition is to  to see them as **applied math problems presented in a musical context.**  A model cannot arrive at the correct answer through passive pattern matching; it must execute a series of computational steps. 
    
    In fact, unlike in domains like pure mathematics or logic, where people can often separate a conceptual understanding problem from a procedural reasoning problem, we argue that in sheet music, understanding and reasoning are deeply intertwined. At the foundational level, the act of understanding is the successful execution of this rule-based reasoning.
    
    Regarding the bar placement example, while the task's description may seem simple (removing bar lines), the reasoning process required to solve it is fundamental to musical comprehension. For a model—or a human student—to correctly place the bar lines in a piece like the one below:
    
    ```
    L:1/8
    M:4/4
    K:D
    ed BG A/B/A/G/ ED GB AG d2 d d/d/ ed BG A/B/A/G/ ED GB A/G/A G2 G d/d/
    ```
    
    It must perform a series of deductive steps:
    
    1. **Identify the Time Signature (M:):** The music is in 4/4 time, meaning each measure must contain the equivalent of four quarter notes.
    2. **Identify the Default Note Length (L:):** The default unit is an eighth note (1/8).
    3. **Calculate Measure Duration:** The model must calculate that a 4/4 measure requires eight 1/8th note units ((4/4) / (1/8) = 8).
    4. **Sum Note Durations:** It must then parse the sequence of notes, correctly calculating the duration of each (e.g., ed = 2 units, A/B/A/G/ = 2 units, d2 = 2 units) and sum them. A bar line is placed only when the sum for a measure reaches exactly 8.
    
    This task demands a model to learn and apply core rules of rhythm and meter. It is not a simple pattern-matching task but a procedural reasoning problem, analogous to skills tested in standardized music theory curricula (e.g., ABRSM).
    
    We present an example of model reasoning to make this process clearer.
    
    **example**: 
    
    ```
    L:1/8
    Q:1/4=120
    M:3/4
    K:F
    f4 F2 g2 gg gg g4 G2 a2 ba gf
    ```
    
    **model response**:
    
    ```
    To determine the correct placement of bar lines in the given sequence of notes, we need to consider the time signature, which is 3/4 in this case. This means each measure must contain exactly three quarter notes (or the equivalent).
    
    Let's analyze the sequence of notes:
    
    L:1/8
    Q:1/4=120
    M:3/4
    K:F
    f4 F2 g2 gg gg g4 G2 a2 ba gf
    
    Breaking it down into smaller segments:
    
    1. f4 F2
    2. g2 gg gg
    3. g4 G2
    4. a2 ba gf
    
    Each segment should contain exactly three quarter notes. Let's count the quarter notes in each segment:
    
    1. f4 F2: 4 (f) + 2 (F) = 6 eighth notes
    2. g2 gg gg: 2 (g) + 2 (gg) + 2 (gg) = 6 eighth notes
    3. g4 G2: 4 (g) + 2 (G) = 6 eighth notes
    4. a2 ba gf: 2 (a) + 2 (ba) + 2 (gf) = 6 eighth notes
    
    Since the time signature is 3/4, each measure must contain exactly three quarter notes. Therefore, the correct placement of bar lines would be after the first and third segments, as they each contain exactly three quarter notes.
    
    The correct option is:
    
    A. L:1/8
    Q:1/4=120
    M:3/4
    K:F
    | f4 F2 | g2 gg gg | g4 G2 | a2 ba gf |
    
    So, the answer is \boxed{A}.
    ```
    
    These reasoning abilities are foundational skills, essential for LLMs to compose sheet music in a manner akin to human musicians.

Thank you for your feedback. We appreciate your concerns; however, we would like to offer a critical clarification regarding the strategic value of our framework and the definition of reasoning in this context.

**1. Limited value of the main contribution (programmatic framework + synthetic data).**

We respectfully argue that utilizing ABC notation is not a limitation, but a core design feature that unlocks Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)—a capability previous works have largely overlooked. Our ultimate goal is to build an AI Musician capable of composition, a task that demands rigorous reasoning. By treating music theory as programmatic functions based on text-based scores (ABC), we can establish a modality-invariant reasoning framework. The logical solution to a music problem remains identical whether the input is text, an image, or audio. Consequently, this allows us to synthesize perfectly aligned, verifiable training data across all modalities (Text, Image, Audio/MIDI). This approach effectively bypasses the noise inherent in Optical Music Recognition (OMR) and the high cost of human annotation, providing the precise "ground truth" signals required to train models to reason via RL, rather than merely recognizing symbols.

**2. “Music reasoning” and “music theory” are poorly defined and weakly evidenced.**

We posit that Musical Reasoning is inherently a domain-specific form of symbolic reasoning. Because sheet music functions as a structured formal language with strict grammatical and mathematical rules, tasks that appear to be simple "calculation" (e.g., interval analysis, rhythmic alignment) are effectively deductive inference steps, analogous to solving mathematical proofs or logic puzzles. We view these tasks as a fundamental case of symbolic reasoning where the model must apply abstract rules to derive correct conclusions. Furthermore, these fundamental operations are non-negotiable prerequisites for high-level musical intelligence. Just as a mathematician cannot solve complex theorems without first mastering arithmetic, an AI cannot perform high-level etiology reasoning or composition without first mastering the "mechanics" of music theory.

As a pioneering work, we focused on these low-level rules in music theory to validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. By demonstrating that models can learn and reason through these fundamental rules, we have laid the necessary groundwork for scaling this verifiable synthesis paradigm to higher-level musical creativity and analysis.

**Our work introduces a new paradigm to address data scarcity in sheet music reasoning.**

By programmatically generating questions based on music theory rules, we transform abstract musical logic into scalable, verifiable computational problems derived from existing sheet music. These problems can then be converted into different modalities by altering the music format. We believe this represents a **groundbreaking** contribution, offering a cost-effective solution to improve LLM and MLLM reasoning in sheet music, ultimately aiding music composition.

While reviewers yS4X, CAkk, and D6f4 acknowledge our novelty and potential, they raised concerns about our focus on low-level music theory. Higher-level music theory and foundational system tools will be addressed in our future work, and we have outlined our research plan and future directions in the rebuttal and the revised paper, which we believe will inspire further exploration in the community.

Additionally, reviewer u888’s concern about the definition and novelty of musical reasoning seems to stem from a misunderstanding in comparing our work to Optical Music Recognition (ORM). The emphasis in our paper is on constructing verifiable problems based on music theory rules from text-based sheet music, which can then be transformed into other modalities.  In this paper, we consider both text and image modalities, and we also plan to extend our research to include MIDI in future studies. Unlike ORM, our primary aim is to enable LLMs to think like musicians.

Finally, we would like to express our sincere gratitude to you and all the reviewers. We hope our work can provide valuable insights and inspiration for the community.
